# Best Medical Chronology Software for Attorneys (2026 Comparison)

March 24, 2026 10 min read

![AI-powered medical chronology organizing treatment records into structured timeline](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/_static/blog/best-medical-chronology-software/hero.png)

Medical chronology software converts unstructured medical records into organized timelines for legal use. For disability law firms, the best options integrate with ERE workflows, support SSD-specific outputs (RFC analysis, treatment compliance), and produce chronologies that serve hearing preparation rather than PI settlement demands.

Every SSD case eventually comes down to the medical records. A single file can run 1,500 pages of treatment notes, imaging reports, and specialist consultations. Paralegals spend 15 to 20 hours organizing that manually. Meanwhile, the hearing date approaches.

Medical chronology software automates most of this. AI extracts dates, diagnoses, providers, and treatments from raw records, then organizes everything into a timeline attorneys can actually use. What took days now takes hours or less.

Here’s the problem: nearly every medical chronology guide on the internet is written for personal injury firms. PI workflows differ from Social Security disability practice in fundamental ways. The tools built for PI may not address what SSD attorneys actually need for hearing preparation.

This guide covers medical chronology software with disability law workflows in mind. It explains what to evaluate, which platforms fit SSD practice, and how medical chronology connects to existing [ERE monitoring](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/blog/how-to-automate-ere-tracking) and case management systems.

## What Medical Chronology Software Does

![AI extraction process - documents to processor to organized output](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/_static/blog/best-medical-chronology-software/body-01.webp)

The process works in stages. You upload records (most platforms accept PDFs, scanned documents, and electronic health record exports). The software runs optical character recognition to read both typed and handwritten notes.

Then comes extraction. AI identifies key data points: patient demographics, appointment dates, diagnoses, procedures, medications, provider names, and clinical findings. The extraction mimics what a paralegal does manually but processes hundreds of pages in minutes.

The output is a structured chronology. Events appear in date order with source citations. Most platforms include page references so you can verify any entry against the original record.

For disability law, the chronology serves a specific purpose: demonstrating how medical evidence supports (or doesn’t support) a claimant’s functional limitations over time.

## Key Criteria for Evaluating Medical Chronology Software

Not all platforms suit every practice. Before comparing features, establish what matters for your firm.

**Accuracy with verification:** extraction accuracy varies. Some platforms claim 95% or higher, but those numbers come from vendor testing. The real test is your records. Can you trust the output without line-by-line review? Look for platforms that cite specific page numbers and allow quick verification.

**Security and compliance:** medical records contain protected health information. Any platform handling PHI needs a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement. Ask about [SOC 2 Type II certification](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/features/secure), encryption standards (AES-256 for data at rest and in transit), and access logging.

**Integration capability:** where does the chronology go after creation? If your workflow involves a case management system or ERE monitoring tool, integration matters. Manual export and re-upload adds friction that compounds over dozens of cases.

**Output format:** some platforms produce dense tables. Others generate narrative summaries. SSD practice often benefits from chronologies that highlight functional limitations, treatment compliance, and gaps in care. Check whether the output format serves your hearing prep process.

**Pricing model:** per-page pricing works for occasional use. Subscription models suit high-volume firms. Some platforms charge per case or per chronology. Calculate your actual cost based on typical file sizes and case volume.

## SSD vs Personal Injury: Different Requirements

![SSD vs PI comparison - single incident versus longitudinal treatment timeline](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/_static/blog/best-medical-chronology-software/body-02.webp)

Most medical chronology guides assume you’re building a personal injury demand package. That assumption shapes the tools they recommend.

PI cases need chronologies that establish causation from a specific incident. Treatment records connect to an accident date. Damages calculations require itemized medical expenses.

SSD cases work differently. The SSA evaluates disability through a [five-step sequential evaluation](https://www.ssa.gov/disability/professionals/bluebook/general-info.htm). Medical evidence must show severity of impairments across at least 12 months, residual functional capacity limitations, treatment compliance and response to care, activities of daily living that corroborate claimed limitations, and consistency between medical findings and subjective symptoms.

An ALJ reviewing your case wants a medical chronology that maps to these questions. A tool optimized for PI settlement packages may not surface the right information.

| Consideration | Personal Injury | Social Security Disability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timeline focus | Single incident to present | 12+ months of treatment history |
| Key evidence | Causation from accident | RFC limitations and severity |
| Output goal | Settlement demand | Hearing preparation |
| Record source | Medical providers, subpoenas | ERE, provider records |
| Typical file size | 200-800 pages | 500-2,000+ pages |

There’s another difference: where records come from. SSD firms pull documents through the ERE (Electronic Records Express), the SSA’s portal for case files and e-folders. Records arrive incrementally as the case progresses. The chronology tool needs to handle records that accumulate over months, not a single document dump.

## Top Medical Chronology Software for Law Firms

The market includes both general-purpose platforms and tools designed for specific practice areas. Here’s how the major options compare for disability law use.

### Dodo (DodoDetect)

Dodo gets the SSD-specific part right. The platform emphasizes RFC analysis support, treatment timeline visualization, and condition severity tracking. Most general-purpose tools miss these entirely.

For firms using Chronicle for ERE monitoring, Dodo offers a direct integration. Records flow from Chronicle into Dodo without manual file transfers. This matters because medical evidence arrives continuously through the ERE; an integrated pipeline reduces handling time and ensures records reach analysis without sitting in download folders.

**Best for:** SSD and workers’ comp firms wanting tight integration with ERE workflows.

### SuperInsight

SuperInsight positions itself as a privacy-first platform with fully automated AI processing. No human reviewers access your documents. The platform generates medical chronologies, summaries, and condition-specific analyses.

Chronicle offers an [API integration with SuperInsight](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/blog/closing-the-loop-ere-to-medical-ai), providing another option for firms that want automated chronology generation connected to their ERE monitoring workflow. The 100% AI approach appeals to firms where data privacy ranks high on the priority list.

The catch: it’s a standalone upload unless you’re using the Chronicle integration. Records don’t flow in automatically from ERE otherwise, so you’re still shuttling files between systems.

### EvenUp MedChrons

EvenUp processes over 1,600 chronologies weekly across 1,500+ personal injury firms. Their model combines AI extraction with human expert review. The platform integrates with major case management systems including Filevine, Litify, and others.

The human review layer adds accuracy verification but also adds time. EvenUp’s primary focus is PI demand packages. SSD firms may find the output format oriented more toward settlement documentation than hearing prep. Worth testing if you handle both practice areas, but probably not the first choice for pure SSD work.

### Filevine MedChron

MedChron lives inside the Filevine ecosystem. If you already use Filevine for case management, the chronology tool connects natively. Upload records and MedChron processes them within your existing workspace.

The platform handles OCR, classification, and chronology generation. It adds Bates numbering automatically. The limitation is obvious: you need Filevine. Firms using other CMS platforms can’t access MedChron as a standalone tool.

### Legalyze.ai

Legalyze offers a subscription model at $150/month with no per-page fees. The platform can process thousands of pages, generating chronologies with page citations. For small firms (or those with high volume but limited budget), the flat pricing stands out.

Integration options include connections to MyCase, Smokeball, CASEpeer, and Litify. The platform isn’t SSD-specific, but the pricing makes it worth testing for disability practices with significant record volume.

### CaseFleet

CaseFleet approaches chronology differently. Rather than pure AI extraction, it emphasizes fact management. You upload records, highlight relevant portions, and the system builds entries from your annotations. AI assists but doesn’t replace human judgment.

For complex SSD cases where nuance matters, this approach offers more control. You decide what enters the chronology. The tradeoff is time: CaseFleet requires more active engagement than fully automated platforms.

### InPractice.ai

InPractice offers a standalone medical review platform. Upload records, receive organized chronologies and summaries. The platform emphasizes speed and handles various document types including handwritten notes.

As a standalone tool, InPractice doesn’t tie you to a specific CMS. It works for firms wanting chronology capability without changing their existing tech stack.

## [How to Choose the Right Medical Chronology Software](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/blog/choosing-the-right-ai-medical-record-platform)

Selecting a platform requires testing with your actual files. Vendor demos use clean, well-organized records. Your cases probably include faxed documents, handwritten notes, and records from multiple providers with inconsistent formats.

Run a real test. Most platforms offer trials. Upload a genuine case file. Compare the output against what a paralegal would produce. Note where the AI missed context, misread dates, or failed to identify key providers.

Check citation accuracy. Every chronology entry should link to a source page. Spot-check entries against the original records. If citations are wrong or missing, the time you save extracting gets spent verifying.

Evaluate integration fit by considering your current workflow: where do records arrive (ERE, direct from providers, client submission)? Where does work happen (CMS, separate intake system, paper files)? Where does the chronology need to go (hearing prep folder, CMS matter, export for counsel)? A chronology tool that doesn’t connect to your other systems creates manual transfer steps. Those steps add time and error opportunity.

Ask about SSD-specific features. Can the platform organize findings by impairment? Does it track treatment compliance over time? Can you filter for RFC-relevant limitations? These features matter for disability law and may not exist in PI-focused tools.

Calculate true cost. Per-page pricing can spike on large files. A 2,000-page case at $0.10 per page costs $200 for one chronology. Subscription models may offer better economics at higher volume. Factor in the number of cases and average record size.

## Medical Chronology in the SSD Workflow

![ERE to chronology pipeline - portal to Chronicle hub to organized output](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/_static/blog/best-medical-chronology-software/body-03.webp)

For disability law, medical chronology fits between record collection and hearing preparation. The timing matters.

Records accumulate throughout a case. Initial applications include existing treatment documentation. As the case progresses through reconsideration and hearing levels, new records arrive. Consultative exam reports. Updated treatment notes. Additional imaging.

Waiting until all records arrive to build a chronology delays hearing prep. Running chronology continuously as records come in keeps the file current.

This is where ERE monitoring connects to medical analysis. Chronicle checks the ERE and e-file daily for each monitored case. When [new medical evidence](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/features/ere-documents) posts, it surfaces immediately. With Chronicle’s Dodo integration, those records can flow directly into chronology generation. No manual downloads. No file transfers. Records move from SSA to analysis without paralegal handling.

At Ficek Law, medical chronology serves as the hearing prep backbone. The firm starts with a high-level summary, then dives into specific records for detailed review. That workflow depends on having current, organized chronologies ready when hearing prep begins.

At Anderson Marois & Associates, the team used medical chronology AI on a case with over 2,000 pages of records. Manually organizing that file would consume multiple paralegal days. Automated chronology made the file workable in a fraction of the time.

The integration point matters: records from ERE flow into analysis without manual transfers. Chronicle supports medical chronology through direct integrations with Dodo and SuperInsight. For SSD firms, this creates a complete pipeline from SSA document monitoring to organized hearing prep materials.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What makes medical chronology software different from manual review?

The difference is extraction speed. Instead of a paralegal reading every page, AI identifies dates, diagnoses, providers, and treatments automatically. The output is a structured timeline with source citations. Manual review still matters for complex entries or ambiguous records, but the bulk of organization happens automatically. At 1,500 pages per file, that distinction determines whether hearing prep starts on time.

### Do SSD cases need different chronology features than PI cases?

Yes. SSD chronologies should track treatment compliance, functional limitations, and condition severity over time. PI chronologies emphasize incident-to-treatment causation and damages. Tools optimized for PI may not highlight what ALJs evaluate under the five-step sequential evaluation. The output format matters as much as the extraction quality.

### How do medical records from ERE connect to chronology tools?

Records in the ERE must be downloaded and uploaded to chronology software. Some firms do this manually per case. With integrated systems like Chronicle connected to Dodo or SuperInsight, records flow automatically from ERE monitoring into analysis without manual file handling. The integration eliminates a step that otherwise repeats for every case, every time new records arrive.

### What security certifications should medical chronology software have?

At minimum: a signed HIPAA Business Associate Agreement. Better platforms hold SOC 2 Type II certification, use AES-256 encryption, and maintain audit logs of who accessed what records. Ask for documentation rather than accepting vendor claims. If they can’t produce the BAA or SOC 2 report, that tells you something.

### How much does medical chronology software cost?

Pricing varies. Per-page models range from $0.05 to $0.25 per page. Subscription models start around $150/month. Per-case or per-chronology pricing also exists. Calculate based on your average file size and case volume to find the actual cost for your practice. A 2,000-page file at $0.10/page is $200 per chronology; at volume, that adds up.

## Conclusion

Medical chronology software handles a task that would otherwise consume paralegal hours. For disability law firms, the right tool connects to existing workflows: records arrive through ERE monitoring, flow into chronology generation, and produce outputs that serve hearing preparation.

Most comparison guides focus on personal injury. That leaves SSD firms evaluating tools without relevant context. The platforms that work best for disability practice offer SSD-specific outputs, integrate with ERE workflows, and produce chronologies organized around what ALJs actually evaluate.

Chronicle supports medical chronology as part of hearing preparation workflows, with direct integrations to Dodo and SuperInsight. For firms already using Chronicle for [ERE monitoring](https://www.chroniclelegal.com/features/ssd-hearing-prep-software), adding medical chronology extends the workflow from document detection through organized analysis.

“Chronicle gives you your best chance to present a good case for a borderline client.” That assessment from Ficek Law reflects what organized medical evidence enables: better preparation, clearer presentation, and stronger hearings.

If you’re evaluating medical chronology software, start with a real test. Upload an actual case file, not a clean demo record. Check how the output serves your hearing prep process. And consider whether the tool connects to how records already move through your firm.

![Building a Persuasive Demand Package with AI](https://provalens.ai/blog/images/provalens-1784505826948.jpg)

A demand package is the first serious conversation your firm has with an insurance adjuster. It sets the tone, establishes credibility, and — when done right — signals that litigation is not a bluff. Yet for most small personal injury firms, assembling that package is one of the most labor-intensive tasks in the entire case lifecycle. Paralegals spend hours cross-referencing medical records, attorneys manually thread together a liability narrative from police reports and witness statements, and the final product is only as thorough as the time budget allows.

AI-powered document intelligence is changing that calculus. Automated medical record review in PI law is no longer a concept reserved for large defense firms with enterprise software budgets. Today, small firms of two to ten attorneys can use the same technology to produce demand packages that are more organized, more internally consistent, and more carefully documented — in a fraction of the time.

This post walks through exactly how that works, from the raw documents on intake to the polished demand letter that lands on an adjuster's desk.

## Why Most Demand Packages Fall Short

Before exploring the solution, it is worth being honest about the problem. Demand packages fail to move adjusters for a handful of predictable reasons.

**Inconsistent chronology.** Medical records arrive from multiple providers — emergency departments, orthopedic surgeons, physical therapists, pain management specialists — often out of order and in different formats. When the damages narrative jumps around in time, it is easier for an adjuster to discount the severity of the injury arc.

**Missed documentation.** A single overlooked billing record or a gap between treatment dates can give a carrier ammunition to argue the client was not as injured as claimed, or that the injury predated the accident. Manual review, especially under deadline pressure, leaves these gaps open.

**Weak liability threading.** Liability and damages are often treated as separate documents that happen to be stapled together. The most persuasive demand packages weave them into a single coherent story: here is what happened, here is why the defendant is responsible, and here is the documented human and financial cost.

**Unsupported special damages.** Adjusters are trained to push back on speculative or loosely supported damage figures. A tally that is not tied to specific line items in the records is an invitation to lowball.

Each of these weaknesses is addressable with the right workflow — and AI accelerates every fix.

## Automated Medical Record Review: What It Actually Does

Automated medical record review in PI law refers to the process of using AI to read, extract, and organize clinical and billing records without requiring an attorney or paralegal to manually page through every document. In practice, this means several concrete things.

### Building the Medical Chronology Automatically

When a firm uploads records to a platform like ProvaLens, the system reads every document — PDFs, scanned pages, handwritten notes processed through OCR — and constructs a chronological timeline of treatment events. Each entry is tagged to the source document, page, and paragraph. The result is a filterable, date-ordered chronology that a paralegal would otherwise spend several hours building.

For a moderately complex PI case with records from four or five providers, the time savings can be substantial. More importantly, the chronology is complete. The AI does not skip the third page of a physical therapy discharge summary because it arrived as a low-resolution scan.

### Itemizing Special Damages with Citations

One of the most powerful applications of automated medical record review in PI law is the generation of an itemized special-damages tally. Rather than manually adding up line items from billing records, the AI extracts each charge, links it to the corresponding treatment date and provider, and produces a damages summary that is fully cited to the underlying records.

This matters in demand negotiations. When an adjuster challenges a line item, your attorney can point to the exact page in the records that supports it. The demand package becomes one the adjuster has to rebut with equal specificity.

### Detecting Gaps and Contradictions

Perhaps the most underappreciated function of automated medical record review is contradiction detection. AI can flag instances where a treatment note contradicts a recorded statement, where a diagnosis in one record conflicts with a notation in another, or where a gap in treatment could be characterized as a break in causation.

Knowing about these issues before the demand goes out allows the attorney to address them proactively — either in the narrative itself or by obtaining additional documentation. Discovering them after the demand goes out, when the adjuster raises them, is a much weaker position.

## Constructing the Liability Narrative with AI Assistance

Damages without liability is a list of expenses. Liability without damages is a grievance. A persuasive demand package fuses the two, and AI tools accelerate both sides of that fusion.

### From Raw Documents to a Coherent Liability Story

ProvaLens reads police reports, witness statements, photographs, recorded statements, and any other documents in the case file and returns answers cited to the exact source. When an attorney asks the system to surface the key liability facts — road conditions, witness accounts of the defendant's behavior, admissions in the recorded statement — the AI retrieves them with citations rather than requiring the attorney to re-read every document.

This is particularly valuable in cases with large document sets. A multi-vehicle accident with three or four witness statements, a lengthy police report, and a recorded statement from the adverse driver can easily run to hundreds of pages. AI chat with citations compresses the research phase dramatically.

### Drafting the Demand Letter Itself

ProvaLens can generate demand letter drafts that incorporate the liability narrative, the medical chronology, and the itemized special damages into a single structured document. The draft is a starting point, not a finished product — the attorney reviews, edits, and applies their judgment and advocacy. But starting from a well-organized, citation-backed draft is fundamentally different from starting from a blank page or a prior demand letter used as a template.

The practical effect is that the attorney's time is spent on the highest-value work: strategy, framing, and negotiation positioning. The mechanical assembly is handled by the AI.

## The Role of Expert Services in High-Stakes Demands

For cases where the damages are significant and the demand package needs to be as airtight as possible, ProvaLens offers Expert Services — a done-for-you AI case analysis. The deliverable includes an interactive timeline, a full medical chronology, and strategic observations prepared by the ProvaLens team. Visit provalens.ai for current pricing and availability.

This service is structured as a genuine out-of-pocket case cost, similar in nature to an expert witness fee or an eDiscovery expense. Firms that choose to pass this cost to the client as a case expense should do so transparently, with client disclosure and informed consent — the same approach used for any third-party case cost. The monthly platform subscription, by contrast, is firm overhead and is not a per-client pass-through.

For a case with complex medical issues, disputed causation, or a high damages ceiling, the Expert Services deliverable can strengthen the demand package. An interactive timeline that an adjuster or opposing counsel can navigate is a different kind of persuasive tool than a static PDF.

## Practical Workflow: From Intake to Demand

Here is what a streamlined demand-package workflow looks like when AI is integrated from the start.

**Intake and document upload.** As records arrive — from providers, from the client, from law enforcement — they are uploaded to ProvaLens. The system classifies documents by type automatically: medical records, billing records, police reports, witness statements, photographs. Documents synced from OneDrive, SharePoint, Google Drive, or Dropbox are imported automatically and trigger re-analysis when updated.

**Chronology and damages tally.** Once the records are substantially complete, the AI generates the medical chronology and itemized special-damages tally. The paralegal reviews for completeness, flags any gaps, and requests additional records if needed.

**Liability research.** The attorney uses AI chat with citations to surface the key liability facts from the police report, witness statements, and any recorded statements. Contradictions and admissions are flagged automatically.

**Draft demand letter.** ProvaLens generates a demand letter draft incorporating the liability narrative, chronology, and damages summary. The attorney edits for tone, strategy, and any case-specific nuance.

**Internal review.** Before the demand goes out, the attorney reviews the full package for internal consistency. The AI's contradiction detection has already done a pass; the attorney's review catches anything that requires professional judgment.

_The following is a hypothetical illustration only._ Imagine a small PI firm handling a soft-tissue motor vehicle case. Using this workflow, the paralegal could spend less time on manual record organization and chronology, and the attorney could begin reviewing a structured demand letter draft earlier in the process — freeing more time for strategy and argument refinement rather than document assembly. Actual time savings will vary by case complexity and firm workflow.

## Consistency Across Every Case

The most important long-term argument for AI-organized demand packages is not the time savings on any individual case. It is the consistency effect across an entire docket.

In a manual workflow, demand package quality varies with workload, deadline pressure, and who happens to be available to work on the file. Some packages are thorough; others are rushed. AI helps raise the baseline. Every case gets a complete chronology, a fully cited damages tally, and a liability narrative built from the actual documents in the file — not from memory or from a template that was last updated two years ago.

For small firms competing against larger defense teams with more resources, that consistency is a meaningful operational advantage. A demand package that is well-organized and internally consistent — with every damages figure tied to a specific record — gives the attorney a stronger foundation for negotiation.

Automated medical record review in PI law is not a future capability — it is available now. If your firm is ready to bring that level of rigor to every demand you send, [Start your free ProvaLens trial](https://provalens.ai/trial.html?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=organic).

## Frequently asked questions

### **What’s the difference between a medical summary and a medical chronology/timeline?**

+

A medical summary provides a plaintiff-focused narrative of treatment, pain, limitations, and recovery. A medical chronology organizes every treatment event chronologically from the incident through Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI). Both are available through Lexee.

### **Does Lexee create the final litigation-ready document?**

+

Lexee delivers a comprehensive draft for internal refinement. Your attorney reviews, verifies details, adds firm-specific emphasis, and approves it before external use. This human-in-the-loop approach ensures every document meets your firm’s quality standards.

### **Does Lexee provide medical opinions or causation analysis?**

+

No. Lexee summarizes and organizes medical information from your case records. It does not provide diagnoses, causation opinions, or clinical interpretations.

### **Can Lexee also retrieve medical records?**

+

Yes. Ask Lexee to retrieve records from providers, and it manages the entire process inside CloudLex—including HIPAA authorization, follow-ups, and status tracking. Records are attached to the correct matter automatically.

### **What happens if records are missing or incomplete?**

+

Lexee flags missing records and creates a checklist of gaps so your team knows exactly what to pursue before finalizing the summary or chronology.

### **How does this relate to Medical Chronology Services?**

+

Lexee AI is the AI-powered capability within CloudLex. Medical Chronology Services, part of paralegal services is the human-expert service offering. Both work together. For the full service experience.

### **Is the output quality dependent on what’s in my case file?**

+

Yes. Lexee works with the records, bills, and notes available in your CloudLex matter. The more complete your case data, the more comprehensive the output.
